title: The executive swipe file.
description: 25 of the best performing posts we published for B2B founders and executives this year, each with its real numbers and the pattern underneath.
formEyebrow: Get it free, in your inbox
disclosure: You will also get The Draft, one letter a week on B2B social and content strategy. Leave whenever you like.

blocks.text: Two posts went out on the same account one day apart. The first, a hiring post, did 15,376 impressions; the second went viral and did 178,179. Yet the hiring post won on followers, saves, comments, sends and profile views.

That pair is why this document exists. Reach is the cheapest number on a post to count, so everyone counts it, and plenty of executives end up grading their content on the number that tells them least.

I'm a partner at RallyUp, where we write LinkedIn for B2B founders and executives. This year the accounts we run did 9.6 million impressions across 24 accounts at 16 companies, from more than 750 posts. This document is the part of that work worth stealing.

Every post in it is real and every number comes from the account's own analytics. I've anonymised the accounts, because the posts belong to the people who published them, and kept the shape of each one: why it worked, and what you can lift without borrowing anyone's words.

items: The intro post that did 1,899 profile views, and why it only works once
A launch that bought 137 hours of attention and fifteen clicks
The two-funnel launch: 554 link clicks and 343 comments from one post
A hiring post with 37 saves and 14 sends, and the filter hidden in the ask
The quarterly self-review that saved at 2.27 per thousand, the highest in the file
Two posts that reached enormous numbers of people and returned nothing

blocks.text: Underneath all of it runs a three bucket model: top of funnel, middle and bottom, roughly 70 / 20 / 10, each graded on a different number. Grade all three on impressions and you'll kill the two that are working.
The limits are in there too. It's 25 posts from 24 accounts, and none of these patterns will hand you a point of view; they move numbers on accounts that already have something to say.
